name: Habetrot

attributes.attribute: British spinner goddess reduced to a fairy spirit after Christianization
healing spirit who could weave garments that protected wearers from illness
appeared as a Fairy Queen who stole unspun flax at the year's end
subject of the Scottish border tale of the lazy girl and seven hanks of yarn

sources: Douglas, George. Scottish Fairy and Folk Tales. West Yorkshire: Ep Publishing, 1977, 109-110.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Habetrot, also spelled Habitrot and called Gyre-Carling or Gy-Carlin, is a British folkloric figure. She began as a spinner goddess. Christianization reduced her to a fairy spirit. She was a healing spirit. Anyone who could make her weave a garment never suffered from illness. In parts of Britain she appeared as a Fairy Queen who stole flax left unspun at the year's end. A Scottish border tale tells of a lazy girl. Her mother told her to finish spinning seven hanks of yarn, and the work hurt her fingers. She wandered to a stream to soothe her hands. There she met an old spinning woman who gave her seven soft hanks spun by ghostly women with twisted mouths. The silky thread drew a handsome lord, who married the girl for her spinning skill. The girl brought her husband to Habetrot. Habetrot showed him the deformed spinners and said her lady would soon look the same. The shocked lord forbade his wife to spin, and she lived the idle happy life she preferred.

okr.objective: Document Habetrot as the British spinner goddess of healing.
